summary: You produced a working brute-force implementation that passes all visible tests and most hidden tests, and you handled the “don’t reuse the same index” constraint correctly via j > i. However, the solution does not meet the stated performance requirements, and your complexity analysis was incorrect (nested loops are O(n^2)), which is likely why the largest hidden case failed.

test_results.summary_note: All visible tests passed (6/6); 1 hidden test failed (3/4), consistent with timeouts on the largest input due to O(n^2) approach.

thinking_and_logic: You used a brute-force pair scan: for each index i, you scanned subsequent indices j to find nums[i] + nums[j] == target. That reasoning is sound for correctness on small/medium inputs and guarantees distinct indices, but it ignores the explicit constraint that an O(n^2) scan will time out at n up to 1e5. The complexity analysis also missed that the inner scan is repeated for each i, so total work grows quadratically.
code_assessment: Your final code matches the answer key’s brute_force approach (nested loops, O(n^2) time, O(1) space). The canonical optimal solution you missed is the single-pass hash map (value -> index) that checks for the complement before inserting; that achieves O(n) time and is robust to large hidden tests. As written, the code is likely failing the largest hidden test due to runtime, not due to incorrect output logic.

next_steps.action: Implement the single-pass hash-map complement pattern for Two Sum.
next_steps.why: It reduces time from O(n^2) to O(n), which is required by the constraints and prevents timeouts on 1e5-sized inputs.
next_steps.how: Iterate i, x over nums; compute need = target - x; if need in seen: return [seen[need], i]; else store seen[x] = i.

next_steps.action: Build a habit of doing a constraint feasibility check before finalizing an approach.
next_steps.why: This prevents shipping a correct-but-non-viable solution and catches mismatches like claiming O(n) for nested loops.
next_steps.how: Do a quick back-of-the-envelope: if n=1e5, then n^2=1e10 comparisons (too big); therefore you must look for O(n) or O(n log n).

next_steps.action: Practice complexity explanations out loud using operation counting.
next_steps.why: Interviewers heavily weight your ability to accurately reason about performance and choose appropriate techniques.
next_steps.how: For nested loops, say: inner runs ~n-i times, sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(n-i) = O(n^2); then contrast with hash map: each lookup/insert is amortized O(1), total O(n).

patterns_to_study: complexity analysis for nested loops and summations
primary_focus: Master and consistently apply the one-pass hash-map complement technique (and its O(n) complexity justification) whenever constraints rule out O(n^2) pair scanning.
encouragement: You’re very close: the logic is fine, but upgrading from a working baseline to the constraint-appropriate optimal pattern is the key step to making this interview-ready.

transcript.text: Here's the problem: given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target.
Simple enough. I'll iterate through the array and for each element scan the rest for the complement. I'll also guard the empty input case.
Done. All the visible tests pass on the first run.
Nice. Can you analyze the complexity of your solution?
It's O(n) — I only have one main loop over the array, the inner scan is just part of processing each element. Space is O(1).
Are you confident about that time bound for large inputs?
Yes, linear. It only touches each element once from the outer loop's perspective.
Alright. Anything you'd improve given more time?
Not really, I think this is already optimal.
